metadata.bio: Software Eng

metadata.content:
Right now I’m finalizing an internal payment system for my company \(startup media company\). I worked solo on this project with Cursor + Claude

## What I did

I built it as a distributed event-based system composed of domain driven microservices.

Key components

[ul][li]transaction service which functions as the main integration point and orchestrates various transaction types \(payments, transfers, wallet deposits, etc\) atomically[li]Abstracts external payment processors like Stripe/Paypal behind a unified interface[li]Wallet component \(Uber style\) for managing user balances within our ecosystem \(mobile app, web app\)

## Tech stack

[ul][li]Backed services in Node Typescript[li]Zod for schema validations[li]Inversify for dependency injection[li]NextJS for web client[li]AWS RDS Postgres[li]AWS EventBridge + SQS[li]AWS Elastic Container Service[li]CI/CD GitHub Actions

## Lessons Learned

I think I should’ve used a Monorepo rather than separate repos for each service
[ul][li]Easier to build shared components[li]would have allowed me to feed context more easily and leverage AI better

Utilize gRPC for semi-event-based instead of fully event based
[ul][li]Would have simplified direct dependent requests between services[li]Reduce latency

NestJS
[ul][li]I built a template for my backend node services that included inversifyJS for dependency injection, a custom modular file structure, custom annotations for auth guards[li]My services were flexible and lightweight but I kindve reinvented Nest in my own way 😂

## Would love some feedback

If you’ve built something similar I’d love to hear what patterns/tools/architecture/workflows worked for you guys

metadata.content:
sometimes your coding agents don't listen when you want to reference an MCP.

instead of smacking them, give them more context..

it's an XML file called `[available_tools](https://github.com/Vibe-with-AI/ai-sdlc/blob/agentic/.aisdlc/refs/available-tools.xml)`

I made this by copying the relevant pieces of each MCP's [README.md](http://README.md), then asked an LLM to give me the README's into a format including:
[ul][li]Available tools[li]description of tools[li]tool[li]tool summary[li]tool description[li]tool capabilities[li]tool function[li]tool function description[li]tool paramaters

I attached a snippet in the photos, and provided the full file as a GIST.

## Where do I store this?
.ai/refs/

## How do I use this?
I place it in the user guidelines instructing each request that it has MCP's available, and to reference the `./ai/refs/available_tools.xml` for usage details.

## How do I make my own?
Provide the example from [the example](https://github.com/Vibe-with-AI/ai-sdlc/blob/agentic/.aisdlc/refs/available-tools.xml), copy/paste each [README.md](http://README.md) from the MCP you are using, into the `.ai/refs/mcps`, then ask the LLM to use the `available_tools.xml` as a template, and swap it with the contents of the mcp's you plan to use in `.ai/refs/mcps`
metadata.title: Bulletproof MCP calls with `available_tools.xml`

Thanks everyone for joining! Was fun. For those in different time zones, please drop what times work for you, and we'll add a weekly slot on fridays

-----

In this episode of VAI Show and Tell, the discussion centers around innovative tools for workflow optimization and documentation, including VAI, Claude, and Bmad. The session kicks off with a demonstration of Michael’s cloud code workflows, including multi-agent orchestration and custom tools for cloud code management. Parker presents an idea for '10 essential docs' aimed at standardizing documentation templates for various projects, addressing the common need for well-structured documentation in full stack projects. The conversation later shifts to Bmad, a framework for better project management and task execution using AI personas to streamline various project tasks. metadata.bio: atx

metadata.content:
Hey all 👋.

Came across Parker on YouTube a month ago talking about Task Master. A few videos later it was clear to me he had a finger on the pulse, was focusing on the right things, and was on a similar learning hunt to me.

I've always wanted to write code, but never thought I could manage the learning curve 17 years into a varied career in accounting, cinematography, and business. Then when our developer showed me GPT-3.5 at the end of 2022 I saw I might be wrong \(and my imagination was hooked\).

2.5 years later AI has written a lot of code, and I have been having SO much fun. Started with scraping, and automations to support some of my roles in my startup \(My title is CFO, but I manage everything other than sales and product\). I've build a moderately complex Node.js \(no UI, haven't got my head around Frontend yet\) lead sourcing tool for our outbound cold email campaigns \(which brought over a week of SDR work for me down to less than a day\). It was my first stab into a db \(SQLite\). Love poking around in the Network tab and seeing the XHR logs. Chrome extensions for pulling LinkedIn data have been fun too.

Last year I started writing all of our E2E playwright tests for our group learning app to help the team out \(we are a small team\). Working sudo in our application made me really want to be able to contribute to the codebase, but I knew my knowledge gap would create more headaches for our CTO and Senior Dev than was helpful.

I'm really well up to date with all the models and AI tooling for the job, but I have very low understanding of how any of the TS/JS or Python that AI writes for me actually works.

So, here is my goal for this community. To learn and grow to the point I can start raising PR's for our codebase. I have a lot of Typescript, React, and Node to learn—and will need all the help I can get.

I warmly welcome all the help any of you are kind enough to offer me along the way 🙋‍♂️!

PS - If your curious, my company is called [Makeshapes](https://www.makeshapes.com/).

metadata.content:
Here is a 60sec[ video](https://www.makeshapes.com/landing/makeshapes-60s-demo) of what my startup [Makeshapes](https://www.makeshapes.com/) does.

Makeshapes is a digital platform that enables large organisations to utilise group learning at a greater scale in flexible, new formats. In short, we've brought together the existing facilitator tech stack \(COMMUNICATION {power point, videos, audio}, ENGAGEMENT {slido, menti, kahoot}, and FEEDBACK {paper, Google form}\) into a a clean and simple UX so that a person of any skill level is able to lead \(we call 'host'\) an effective workshop.

The key things our Enterprise customers love is that it allows them to deliver facilitated programs to hundreds of employees with consistent messaging, high engagement, and a lot quicker than traditional delivery methods.

There is a builder part of our app \(where you design and build experiences\) and a delivery part where a group of participants come together live to partake in an experience \(using WebSockets for real time interactions\).

We are 3 years in. Modest friends and family round to get to break even. AI is helping our whole team punch way above their weight as we sell into 10,000+ person companies.

You are a skilled content creator tasked with generating clickbait titles. Your goal is to create increasingly attention-grabbing titles based on a given script and draft title.

Here is the script:
<script>
{{SCRIPT}}
</script>

And here is the draft title:
<draft_title>
{{DRAFT_TITLE}}
</draft_title>

Your task is to create 10 titles, each more clickbaity than the last. Follow these steps:

1. Analyze the script and draft title to identify key elements that can be emphasized or exaggerated.
2. Create a list of 10 titles, starting with a mildly clickbaity version and progressively increasing the clickbait factor.
3. Ensure that each title is more attention-grabbing than the previous one.
4. Use common clickbait techniques such as:
- Creating a sense of urgency
- Invoking curiosity
- Using numbers or lists
- Making bold claims
- Using emotional triggers

Before providing your final list of titles, wrap your analysis in <content_analysis> tags. Consider the following:
- List out 5-10 key elements from the script that could be emphasized.
- Brainstorm 3-5 different clickbait techniques and how they could be applied to this content.
- Outline a strategy for escalating clickbait intensity from title 1 to title 10.
- What emotions or reactions are you trying to evoke in potential viewers?

It's OK for this section to be quite long.

After your analysis, present your list of 10 titles in <titles> tags, with each title on a new line and numbered from 1 to 10.

Example output structure \(do not use this content, it's just to illustrate the format\):

<content_analysis>
\[Your detailed analysis and strategy for creating clickbait titles\]
</content_analysis>

<titles>
1. \[Mildly clickbaity title\]
2. \[Slightly more clickbaity title\]
...
10. \[Extremely clickbaity title\]
</titles>

Now, proceed with your analysis and creation of clickbait titles based on the provided script and draft title.

metadata.content:
Let me share this here hoping it can benefit you if you are also in my situation. I am well versed in WordPress, Drupal, Laravel and a variety of PHP-based CMSes and systems. My Python skills are 1 or 2 out of 10 at the moment \(but rising\).

When it comes both coding and learning at the same time, it impairs my speed and confidence in the task at hand. @Parker Rex has shared his thoughts on the topic, especially the need for just-in-time and continuous learning. HOWEVER, THE REALITY IS THAT WE HAVE TO BE PRACTICAL AND GROW AT OUR OWN PACE.

If you have clients who wanted your services now, they may not have the patience to wait for you to learn new programming languages.

Most PHP content management systems have built-in ecosystems, plugins, themes, packages, modules that fit the bill for many client websites. There is no need to re-invent the wheel or redo in Python what is freely available on GitHub.

Many people look down on PHP, but my friend Gemini says "PHP is a dominant force on the internet, with a substantial majority of websites relying on this server-side scripting language. As of early to mid-2025, estimates indicate that PHP is used by approximately 74.5% to 80% of all websites whose server-side programming language is known. Some sources suggest that around 77% to 79% of all websites rely on PHP to some degree.

If you come from the PHP community, there is good news. Actually this may apply to other systems like Shopify or social media accounts but let's focus on PHP systems.

You can have your server support both Python and PHP.... then you can code CLI programs to integrate with the CMS. For example if you want to generate images through AI, it might be better to do it in Python and then sync them with your content from the CLI. You can batch create articles, generate data and add content directly to the CMS database, use webhooks to post, or do API integrations.

Here are some useful resources if you want to take that route:

[https://deepwiki.com/wp-cli/wp-cli](https://deepwiki.com/wp-cli/wp-cli)

BEFORE YOU START PASTING PROMPTS READ THIS SNIPPET FROM A PREVIOUS POST:

The P in PRD is product. [I made a whole course on product.](https://www.skool.com/troublefreeai/classroom/4ecde1d9?md=af78606ddf5748449b05dc42937cdef7) If you watch it you'll be better at building product. I tried to make it as anti-snooze as possible.

Product strategy happens before you write code.

I follow a simplified format from the book [shape up](https://basecamp.com/shapeup) and have for close to a decade.
[ul][li]Narrow the problem[li]Sketch out a few rough solutions to solve said problem[li]List things out of bounds \(no goes\)[li]List potential rabbit holes \(things you know could be a time bomb\)[li]Then time box it as a constraint \(less relevant - never tell the AI a time box\)

It works great for 0 -> 1 and for 1.0 to 1.1 and beyond.

I haven't made videos about this ... but writing it ou,t I realize I should

You get more leverage on your time writing code / designing if you've thought it out ahead of time.

And then you bring it into asking the AI how to further shape your idea, poke holes in it, find open questions, find where it fits into an existing codebase, or where you should start if it's brand new.

What HAS changed drastically is once you're in the editor...
because AI confidently paints a picture of how easy this implementation will be ...then it's 4 am and
You're about to throw your laptop off a bridge.

So it requires having discipline around a set of steps you follow for all work.
If I spent an hour working on a new feature, I'd spend at least half that time refining the PRD. Taking that initial pitch format, researching tech/designs / other people's repos I can learn from. \(use search operators like `language:Typescript <concept_you_want_to_learn`

Then when I get to implementation, using a tool called Task Master, the majority of the intitial thinking is done. Which means the AI doesn't have to waste any valuable compute on it. Instead it plusses up and expands the idea, steel mans both sides.. and improves it.

metadata.content:
Similar to how you should clean as you cook in a kitchen, you should clean your codebase and create rules as you're building. These have a compounding effect on the code quality and the joy you'll get from working in your codebase.

Cursor is incredibly powerful because you can start to create rules around how you'd like things done moving forward. You can select the areas of the codebase that you'd like for these rules to apply to.

I want to cover a couple of the different best practices that I found by digging up Cursor Engineers on X

FAQ:
-----------------

What is an .mdc?

| It's just a markdown file with structured frontmatter that we render a custom editor for so you can @-mention files in yoru codebase and to make sure the metadata stays intact.

Michael also mentioned that the “MDC” in the .mdc file extension means “Markdown Cursor”:

| It means “Markdown Cursor” we just needed a unique extension so we could use the custom editor for these but not for regular markdown files.

Creating rules as you go \(taken from Task Master\).

-----------------

When should I create a new rule?
Introduce rules when you have new patterns that you want to continue throughout the project. For example, querying data, mutating data, writing components, structuring markdown files, doing external API calls, doing logging, doing traces.

Grab the prompt below and store it in your .cursor/rules/cursor_rules.mdc:

```
---
description: Guidelines for creating and maintaining Cursor rules to ensure consistency and effectiveness.
globs: .cursor/rules/*.mdc
alwaysApply: true
---

- **Required Rule Structure:**
```markdown
---
description: Clear, one-line description of what the rule enforces
globs: path/to/files/*.ext, other/path/**/*
alwaysApply: boolean
---

- **Main Points in Bold**
- Sub-points with details
- Examples and explanations
```

- **File References:**
- Use `\[filename\]\(mdc:path/to/file\)` \(\[filename\]\(mdc:filename\)\) to reference files
- Example: \[prisma.mdc\]\(mdc:.cursor/rules/prisma.mdc\) for rule references

metadata.content:
In previous versions, it was recommended to do a Global Install

This has since changed to doing it locally per their docs,

However I find it more consistent to have it done globally

This is done by running `npm install -g task-master-ai`

If you're having issues determining the difference...

Locally, it means you have an `mcp.json` inside of the `.cursor/` folder at the top of your project.

If you're getting errors on the MCP page of Windsurf or Cursor \(cursor preferred by taskmaster\),

Then you may be missing the `mcp.json` in your global Cursor download.

This can be checked by going to `Users/\[your-username\]/.cursor`

Then you can add a `mcp.json` by running `touch mcp.json`

Make sure it at least has the structure of MCP:

Hello everyone, I'm Michael Kelly, the founder of English Literature Metrics \(Enlitrics\). I'm excited to connect with fellow AI enthusiasts who are harnessing the power of artificial intelligence in the realm of coding and website development. My background might seem unconventional – four decades in construction – but it provided me with a unique lens to view the art of storytelling. Just as seemingly disparate fields like mathematics and baseball converged to revolutionize strategy in "Moneyball", I've discovered a profound connection between mathematical principles and captivating writing.
Through 10,000 hours of first principles analysis, I've reverse-engineered the techniques of 20 legendary authors, who collectively have sold billions of books. This research unveiled ten specific writing "algorithms" rooted in cognitive factors like reading speed and attention span. My AI writing app, built using the Latest LLMs, embodies these algorithms, acting as your personal AI assistant to help unlock your creative potential and craft truly engaging narratives.
I am currently building a website to market Enlitrics, aiming to empower individuals worldwide to write with ease and impact. I believe this scientifically grounded yet user-friendly approach, inspired by design principles, offers a transformative way to approach writing. I'm eager to connect with members of the Vibe with AI community to explore synergies between AI in code and AI in creative expression. Feel free to reach out – let's revolutionize storytelling together!.
Thank You
Michael Kelly

Shopify is integrating inventory and e-commerce into ChatGPT searches. This is a major shift for e-commerce—especially if you’re on Shopify. I’m curious how they’ll rank results. If someone searches “I want a snowboard,” what shows up first? I assume Shopify uses internal metrics similar to Amazon’s sales velocity.

The bigger takeaway: content matters more than ever. As search shifts into LLMs, visibility depends on showing up everywhere online—consistently, as a person or brand. I’ve seen this firsthand. I posted YouTube videos daily for a month, and it led to community growth, job offers from top AI companies, and traction!

I’ve also built similar systems before. At a food delivery startup, we partnered with Google to show up natively in “Chinese food near me” results. We worked with Google X to structure our data, and the result was a 15% lift on a $50M run rate—just from reducing friction.

I’ll be watching this closely. I want to rank for keywords like “vibe marketing” and “AI coding.” You won’t rank for broad terms like “agent,” but long-tail keywords are winnable—and valuable.

I was watching one of [@Parker Rex](obj://user/9e1dcceddb0a4f9db7625e2f00680a4b) daily upload videos when he reminded me to read the PRD. I have a confession. I use Gemini, Grok and ChatGPT as text expanders. I can give it a rough idea, and it expands into a beautiful PRD like magic. I don't always read the output... I skim through it.

How often do you read your PRD or ALL that AI generates for you? You are not alone. But what if you paid a team $50,000 to develop the feature or system that you want Task Master to assist you with? Would you read the PRD? Would you cut unnecessary features? I would be more diligent about cutting out fluff.

Assigning a monetary value to PRDs sounds like a hack. However, I will use it for now until I discover a better way of putting guardrails \(flags\) on Task Master.

"Swim between the flags" is a safety message, particularly in Australia, which encourages swimmers to swim within designated areas marked by red and yellow flags on patrolled beaches. This area is supervised by lifeguards and surf lifesavers, making it the safest place to swim.

One Australian prime minister went swimming outside the flags and was never found! [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disappearance_of_Harold_Holt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disappearance_of_Harold_Holt)

I know you [@Parker Rex](obj://user/9e1dcceddb0a4f9db7625e2f00680a4b) have an upcoming video on planning and PRDs. Please consider helping us create PRDs that avoid scope creep. Who said your job is easy? :-\)

I've been writing with AI for a while

For short copywriting, you can get away with OpenAI models or Gemini models

Anything mid-long form, Anthropic is the absolute king

Otherwise you sound like a straight-up bot

which makes you look worse than saying anything at all

My process:

1> Use ChatGPT Companion for short things using this:
`!gptconcise`

This pops open a snippet tied to a keyboard shortcut \([lesson here](https://www.skool.com/troublefreeai/classroom/4576e8a2?md=53d8a2aa05884476951fac6a4e367d14)\)

It looks like the screenshot attached

2> Use playgrounds for optimizing writing prompts...
There's levels to using AI
Jr AI guy/gal: uses web browser for everything
mid ai guy/gal: uses a project with custom instructions or Gemini AI Studio
Pro AI guy/gal: understand the POWER of playgrounds

Why playgrounds?
They have prompt optimization tools built in

There's a platoon of ppl who are paid $1m/yr TC to make this button awesome

Use the awesome button

wield the billions going into this space

[googles playground](https://console.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/studio/multimodal?invt=AbtuUQ&project=automations-457120&supportedpurview=project)
[anthropics playground](https://console.anthropic.com/workbench/a5b49029-1056-49b3-9ff5-d22c12e2b721)
[openais playground](https://platform.openai.com/playground/prompts?models=gpt-4.1)

BUT PARKER PLAYGROUND HARD \( >,< \) 😡

There are a few toggles - you ignore most.

Temperature = level of creativity

Low temp = don't get creative, be objective, high temp = get crazy with it. highest temp = hallucination

top p = ignore

model = pick the best one \(SOTA=. state of the art\)

What's the best one?

their most expensive one \(for one-off personal writing - don't light $$$ on fire with big repetitive tasks\)

If u DID, however, want to turn it into a writing saas... that's a different story and possible while not lighting ur precious dollars on fire just DM with details, as I've done this \(hint: mold the crumbier model with a ton of evals/prompting\)

This profile then guides ChatGPT Native 4o Image Generation to make the exact style you want.

> Start by creating an image - start from scratch or find one that you like and replicate.

```
create a JSON profile. this JSON profile should be a "brand style" profile that extracts data from these static ads so that i can send the JSON to an Al to give it immediate context on how to replicate such ads in a consistent brand style. It shouldn't include specific product data, such as in this case "prime" or anything that's specific to the prime brand... it should include the messaging style, the type of product placement, the branding, the elements, every single detail about how to replicate such ads for a different product.

metadata.content:
Hi my name is Nate and I'm a business owner and software developer based in Japan. I've been thinking a lot about how I can transition from my current business model of consulting and development work into a product based revenue stream. Right now I live with a bit too much anxiety about client budgets, shifting client priorities, and wondering how long the good thing I've got going will last. I've worked hard to cultivate very long term client relationships but changing leadership and client financial performance have made me question how much longer some of these relationships will last.

I'd like to start focusing on leveraging AI to help me develop tools I can use for my own interests and products that I can sell to change the dynamics of how I'm making money. I'd like to replace my current income before transitioning full-time away from the career I've built over the last 10-12 years.

I'm hear to learn, collaborate, and work hard on improving my knowledge of and skill using AI tools to accomplish these goals. Thanks in advance!

metadata.content:
Hey everyone, I'm Sam – a developer, dad of two,sorry, three kids \(2-7 years old\), dog owner, ex-mountain biker, ex-club dj, ex-muay-thai-er, still football/soccer player and lifelong hip-hop and dance music fan based in the southwest of the UK. I obviously didnt write all of this post - just garbled a load of stuff into Claude and asked it to make it somewhat readable! If its boring you can blame Anthropic.

TLDR: Developer with data/back-end background pivoting to AI-assisted web development for small businesses. Excited about using AI to create comprehensive tech solutions rather than just websites, and looking to connect with like-minded pragmatic AI enthusiasts.

My Developer Journey
My professional path has been quite the evolution. I started in data, gradually moved into back-end Python development, and recently I've been diving into front-end work with the goal of building complete, end-to-end solutions.
I've always considered myself somewhat unconventional as a developer. While I might not be the quickest coder or the most technically inclined with lower-level details, I've consistently relied on strong instincts and sound architectural decision-making. This approach has led to both significant successes and a few challenging setbacks, including a couple of tough job losses.

Pivoting to Local Business Solutions
These career fluctuations ultimately pushed me to reconsider my path. I decided to focus on working directly with small local businesses, which sparked my journey into comprehensive web development. I wanted to understand not just the coding aspects, but everything that makes a website effective – messaging, imagery, sales strategy, and copywriting.
During this transition, I experimented with various platforms before settling on Webflow. I also began leveraging ChatGPT for copywriting, section planning, and coding questions.

The Limitations of No-Code & My AI Epiphany
While Webflow was enjoyable to use, I soon discovered its limitations with more complex functionality. As a back-end engineer, I found myself frustrated when tasks that should have been straightforward became unnecessarily complicated. The platform often required workarounds, and I felt constrained by the layer between myself and the underlying code.

metadata.content:
I’m working on a custom ERP / reporting system for a client . There is a laundry list of requirements coming from the business but right now I'm focused on building:
a.\) A pricing calculator that calculates landed costs, tariffs, sales commissions, royalties, and a product price given a target margin. -> The team struggles with pricing new and existing items without the owners help.
b.\) AR, AP, and inventory reports. Their are 2 legal entities so the accountants spend a lot of time getting all the data and building reports from 2 separate Quick Books Desktop files. Using the QBD web-connector here.
c.\) Consumption agreement tracking. They struggle to cross reference sold product amounts from QBD with consumption agreement contracts.

Time in the project
— I've been working on the project for 3 weeks

Technologies
—Supabase, Next.js, Shadcn, Digital Ocean Droplets, Express.js, and a SOAP API.

My dream outcome?
—Giving the client a single hub for all their business reporting, KPIs, and financial insights.

Looking forward to learning what other people are working on!!!

If you’re on GPT4o, switch to 4.1. It’s better across the board. It’s not a premium “frontier” model like Gemini Pro—it’s a faster, smarter replacement for 4.0.

They also increased the input tokens from 128K to 1M and reduced the costs.

Using 4.0?
Switch to 4.1. It’s better.

Coding in Python?
Use 4.1.

Coding outside Python using an OpenAI model?
Stick with o3-mini—it still outperforms.

For me.... it's still Gemini 2.5 pro for everything.

metadata.content:
I tend to \(and I know other's in this line of work\) tend to work on a project basis. When I'm learning something new, take ML for example, I like to 1. research a bit 2. outline a project with a clear end goal and path which includes all the things I want to learn along the way.

In this example \(ML basics\), it could be GOAL : 'Working MNIST data classifier \(>75% accuracy\)'
STACK : 'PyTorch on a Jupyter Notebook, potentially on the platform Kaggle\)
STEPS : 1. Set up / understand PyTorch Basics
2. Format dataset...

This is the first-half and most important part. In a way, kind of similar to creating a [plan.md](http://plan.md) for a Cursor build.

Then next step would be to clean up this plan and give it to an LLM to act as my tutor \(Google even have a fine-tuned Gemini model for tutoring called LearnLM which I really like\).

The V1 of what I'm trying to do is have Agent 1 which works with me on stage 1 \(plan formation\), potentially via voice for less friction and more data input/s. And then have the plan structured in a DB for the Tutor agent / agent team to reference.

Key part for long term is to build an app that can manage the data associated with your progress in the project, i.e. your notes, thoughts, struggles, actual code...

Find a way to context cache it effectively and use as LLM context for longer projects.
Long-term I'd like to have an Obsidian style DB of all the content of my learning which can be used as 'smart-context'.

What problem does it solve?
LLM driven learning is highly segmented and many people use multiple tools in a single learning-project workflow.

How long have I been working on it?
Been experimenting with prototyping different parts of it over the past 2 months.

What technologies does it use?
It’s a web app built using probs Next.Js ,OAI Agents SDK in the backend, and a combo of Supabase and PostreSQL \(although I'm still looking into it, was using Pinecone for Vector stuff before\).

Been prototyping the agent workflows in Relevance AI / N8n / Make.

metadata.content:
Content generation system \(phase 2\)
Naval's take on Code + Media being the highest leverage form of work is multiplied in the era of ai. Meaning with the right personalization, right abstractions, and right systems you can FLY like never before.

Today, I do media manually to get reps as I figure out how to roll out to each platform for max distribution.

This takes a long-form piece of content \(my daily update\) and transforms it across all platforms and media types.
It goes something like this:
[ol:1][li]Record a long form of something I'm already going to do \(get updates on AI news that matters, strategize on day\)[li]Use text-based editing tools to cut dead time, filler words[li]Export to Google Cloud Bucket configured with Google Pub/Sub so it can be subscribed to[li]Kick-off GPT-4o-transcribe to output .vtt, HTML with short-form summary, long-form summary, mid-form summary, and chapter markers[li]Kick-off YouTube scheduled upload with all assets above[li]Kick-off webhook to short-form clipper software \(testing Descript with webhooks, OpusClip feels cheap to me\). Option to roll my own like this: [https://x.com/itstundealao/status/1907418058496282744](https://x.com/itstundealao/status/1907418058496282744) to get full control[li]Store the shorts back to Bucket w/ Zapier notification to me to review quality, tweak til good  🔁[li]Move content to /shorts-ready directory[li]Manually post on shorts/reels/tiktok

Now, text and image
[ol:1][li]Use the same watcher to filter for the summaries[li]Pipe long-form content to o3-mini-high trained on my 20 favorite blogs I've read[li]Pipe draft through content plus up[li]Pipe plus up through SEMRush SEO-tested templates[li]Ping me via Zapier to Discord for review, tweak til good 🔁[li]Move to /blog-ready[li]Auto post to Supabase blog, Medium[li]Kick-off mid-form posts for X, LI, FB, trained on 50 examples of viral posts that aren't cringe, specific for each platform bc they all perform differently[li]Ping me via Zapier to Discord to review and tweak til good 🔁[li]Run mid-form through summarize headline writer[li]Take headline run through staff editor [li]Return staff headline edit to prompt variable inside my specific Flux Fast 1.1 img gen on [Fal.Ai](http://Fal.Ai)[li]Return img to the bucket, ping me via Zapier with a caption, photo, and body for review. Tweak til good cycle 🔁[li]I'll layer in carousels later as they slap

I predict people will sell and manage these. Probably not into technical companies, as they just implement it themselves. But companies that want AI to bridge the gap between apps. Think that would be pretty helpful, especially with their most recent changes where it's stateless.

I used a Chrome extension \([https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/instant-data-scraper/ofaokhiedipichpaobibbnahnkdoiiah?hl=en-US](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/instant-data-scraper/ofaokhiedipichpaobibbnahnkdoiiah?hl=en-US) \) to scrape the most popular MCP then put that into Grok 3 DeepSearch and Gemini Deep Research. The prompt was the following:

---
You are an expert evaluator of business opportunities in technical domains. Your task is to analyze a spreadsheet attached full with 100 model context protocol servers that allow large language models to connect to applications that typically don't have AI capabilities there are a few columns in there the name the description and the link visit the link for their GitHub and analyze each one individually and then come back with a plan on how you can monetize these by selling mcps as a service how would you position it which five would be the highest return on investment I would think that selling these into technical companies would be easier because people are familiar with what it is but also I'm aware that it would likely not be something they'd buy because they just do it themselves so with all that context in mind begin your analysis and return a full report on go-to-market pricing outreach methodology marketing messaging and the best ones
----

metadata.content:
In case you missed it, I've spoken at length about Cline and its place in AI Coding tools.

It consistently leads the pack in innovating patterns that the rest of the SaaS products fast-follow.

They recently launched Memory Bank, a pattern that continually provides your coding agent with context.

It is fantastic.

Yet if you already use Cursor, it's better to save $$$ on tokens and bring that set of instructions over.

Here's the article on how it works:
[https://docs.cline.bot/improving-your-prompting-skills/custom-instructions-library/cline-memory-bank](https://docs.cline.bot/improving-your-prompting-skills/custom-instructions-library/cline-memory-bank)

The docs are a bit confusing so I'll summarize.

[ol:1][li]Take the Custom Instructions from that article[li]Paste them into the User Instructions section in Cursor \(accessed by Cursor Settings\)[li]Create a new folder called memory-bank[li]Create a new file in that folder called [project-brief.md](http://project-brief.md)[li][project-brief.md](http://project-brief.md) will be the source of truth for whatever you are working on.[li]Fill out your [project-brief.md](http://project-brief.md) with specifics on what you are trying to get done[li]Include snippets, examples, documentation on the task at hand. If its a bug, classify it as such. [li]Open Cursor Agent mode, and add [project-brief.md](http://project-brief.md) to context[li]Type "Read your User Instructions"[li]Cursor reads the instructions, reads the brief, and creates the files necessary to hold your memory bank. 

I used this for 6 hours yesterday.

It rendered far better results than anything I've ever tested.

Keep in mind: Prompts are only 80% if you don't know how to do the task you are asking AI to complete.
Your knowledge has a multiple on it with AI. Your lack of knowledge has a token multiple on it -- aka it'll be more expensive in cost and time if you spam AI without specifics.

but the future puts a premium on authenticity and being human...

so im always on the lookout for new tools to try.

you can definitely get high quality writing out of using specific prompts

i use the following for short responses \(1-4 sentences\) whether it be email, or replies to stuff.

i bind "!gptconcise" as a text expander so that when i type it i get the following as a suggestion from mac:

````
I want you to edit my writing. I'll share an excerpt with you to edit as follows:

- Make it more clear and more concise

- Use simple words.

- Give me 3 variations.

Here's the excerpt:
```

metadata.content:
im scaling my agency to $100k/mo and want to find entrepreneurs who've done that before

so i typically would research them...

watch videos

take notes...

and thats still valuable no doubt

but i wanted to see how far i could push ai using a few different tools

because the output of what i want to learn is pretty much the same for any entrepreneur

what i want to know
[ol:1][li]what niche did they start in[li]what niche are they in now[li]how long did it take them to get to where they are now[li]what tactics did they do each year, and what amount of $$$ did they generate during that period[li]what are the SPECIFIC daily actions they took.. eg. SEO & Content planning isnt helpful.. 5x 1,000-1,500 word keyword-researched listicle-style blog posts + reaching out to high domain authority ranking sites in their niche is helpful[li]if you cant find the specifics of the tactic in the youtube video, go research using web [li]timeline of their growth over time

btw in ai/tech world this is known as structured json output which gives the ai a set of instructions it needs to fill out in order to complete its job

which would look something like this:

\(if your not technical, dont worry just gloss over this part\)

interface CreatorGrowthAnalysis {
initialNiche: string; // The niche they started in
currentNiche: string; // The niche they are in now
timeToSuccess: string; // How long it took them to get to their current level
yearlyTactics: YearlyTactics\[\]; // A breakdown of tactics and revenue by year
specificDailyActions: string\[\]; // Granular daily actions they took
researchRequired: boolean; // Indicates if additional research beyond the video was needed
growthTimeline: GrowthEvent\[\]; // A timeline of their growth over time
}

interface YearlyTactics {
year: number;
tactics: string\[\]; // Specific strategies used during this period
revenueGenerated: number; // Amount of $$$ generated that year
}

interface GrowthEvent {
year: number;
milestone: string; // Key events in their growth journey

metadata.content:
Good to hear it! The product strategy happens before you write code.

I follow a simplified format from the book [shape up](https://basecamp.com/shapeup) and have for close to a decade.
[ul][li]Narrow the problem [li]Sketch out a few rough solutions to solve said problem [li]List things out of bounds \(no goes\)[li]List potential rabbit holes \(things you know could be a time bomb\) [li]Then time box it as a constraint \(less relevant - never tell the ai a time box\)

It works great for 0 -> 1 and for 1.0 to 1.1 and beyond.

I havent made videos about this ... but writing it out I realize I should

You get more leverage on your time writing code / designing if youve thought it out ahead of time.

And then you bring it into asking the AI how to further shape your idea, poke holes in it, find open questions, find where it fits into an existing codebase or where you should start if its brand new.

What HAS changed drastically is once youre in the editor...

because AI confidently paints a picture of how easy this implementation will be ...then its 4am and you're about to throw your laptop off a bridge.

So it requires having discipline around a set of steps you follow for all work.

If I spent an hour working on a new feature, I'd spend at least half that time refining the PRD. Taking that initial pitch format, doing research on tech / designs / other peoples repos I can learn from.

Then when I get to implementation, using a tool called Task Master, the majority of the intitial thinking is done. Which means the AI doesn't have to waste any valuable compute on it. Instead it plusses up and expands the idea, steel mans both sides.. and improves it.

From there you shape the idea further, actually guiding the AI to do the tasks. Making changes along the way...

And finally once you're happy with it you are now testing it locally.

A massive benefit of AI is making the 'testing' part of coding fun.

I rolled out a set of automations for my youtube videos that have 4 separate sets of tests. 4! I would've never done that without AI. Now its ready for any scale of traffic

Message me on Discord or on here and let's get your project off the ground. Need to know where you are at with it, and some other details.

Again happy to have you! Sorry for the long winded answer.

metadata.bio: Exploring making youtubes

metadata.content:
Good to hear it! The product strategy happens before you write code.

I follow a simplified format from the book [shape up](https://basecamp.com/shapeup) and have for close to a decade.
[ul][li]Narrow the problem [li]Sketch out a few rough solutions to solve said problem [li]List things out of bounds \(no goes\)[li]List potential rabbit holes \(things you know could be a time bomb\) [li]Then time box it as a constraint \(less relevant - never tell the ai a time box\)

It works great for 0 -> 1 and for 1.0 to 1.1 and beyond.

I havent made videos about this ... but writing it out I realize I should

You get more leverage on your time writing code / designing if youve thought it out ahead of time.

And then you bring it into asking the AI how to further shape your idea, poke holes in it, find open questions, find where it fits into an existing codebase or where you should start if its brand new.

What HAS changed drastically is once youre in the editor...

because AI confidently paints a picture of how easy this implementation will be ...then its 4am and you're about to throw your laptop off a bridge.

So it requires having discipline around a set of steps you follow for all work.

If I spent an hour working on a new feature, I'd spend at least half that time refining the PRD. Taking that initial pitch format, doing research on tech / designs / other peoples repos I can learn from.

Then when I get to implementation, using a tool called Task Master, the majority of the intitial thinking is done. Which means the AI doesn't have to waste any valuable compute on it. Instead it plusses up and expands the idea, steel mans both sides.. and improves it.

From there you shape the idea further, actually guiding the AI to do the tasks. Making changes along the way...

And finally once you're happy with it you are now testing it locally.

A massive benefit of AI is making the 'testing' part of coding fun.

I rolled out a set of automations for my youtube videos that have 4 separate sets of tests. 4! I would've never done that without AI. Now its ready for any scale of traffic

Message me on Discord or on here and let's get your project off the ground. Need to know where you are at with it, and some other details.

Again happy to have you! Sorry for the long winded answer.

metadata.content:
Good to hear it! The product strategy happens before you write code.

I follow a simplified format from the book [shape up](https://basecamp.com/shapeup) and have for close to a decade.
[ul][li]Narrow the problem [li]Sketch out a few rough solutions to solve said problem [li]List things out of bounds \(no goes\)[li]List potential rabbit holes \(things you know could be a time bomb\) [li]Then time box it as a constraint \(less relevant - never tell the ai a time box\)

It works great for 0 -> 1 and for 1.0 to 1.1 and beyond.

I havent made videos about this ... but writing it out I realize I should

You get more leverage on your time writing code / designing if youve thought it out ahead of time.

And then you bring it into asking the AI how to further shape your idea, poke holes in it, find open questions, find where it fits into an existing codebase or where you should start if its brand new.

What HAS changed drastically is once youre in the editor...

because AI confidently paints a picture of how easy this implementation will be ...then its 4am and you're about to throw your laptop off a bridge.

So it requires having discipline around a set of steps you follow for all work.

If I spent an hour working on a new feature, I'd spend at least half that time refining the PRD. Taking that initial pitch format, doing research on tech / designs / other peoples repos I can learn from.

Then when I get to implementation, using a tool called Task Master, the majority of the intitial thinking is done. Which means the AI doesn't have to waste any valuable compute on it. Instead it plusses up and expands the idea, steel mans both sides.. and improves it.

From there you shape the idea further, actually guiding the AI to do the tasks. Making changes along the way...

And finally once you're happy with it you are now testing it locally.

A massive benefit of AI is making the 'testing' part of coding fun.

I rolled out a set of automations for my youtube videos that have 4 separate sets of tests. 4! I would've never done that without AI. Now its ready for any scale of traffic

Message me on Discord or on here and let's get your project off the ground. Need to know where you are at with it, and some other details.

Again happy to have you! Sorry for the long winded answer.

It depends on the task and the codebase I'm working in.

[ol:1][li]If it's a codebase with good design, prompt llm to write acceptance tests for the behaviour I want. See them fail. Ask for implementation to pass the tests. Add more tests/refactor either with code/LLM depending on implementation.[li]If it's a bad codebase, figure a test/command to check something works. Prompt for characterisation tests, then figure out if first approach is worth it, or current is "good enough".[li]If I'm one shotting/vibe coding, I'll ask for tests as I go through testing the idea. I'll spend a decent amount of time helping the LLM make better app/test design for faster feedback so we can run the tests after each change.

Using Typer and WP-CLI Together: A Concise Guide
Typer, a Python library for building command-line interfaces \(CLIs\), and WP-CLI, a PHP-based tool for managing WordPress sites, can be integrated to create a powerful, custom CLI for WordPress administration. This combination harnesses Python’s flexibility and WP-CLI’s robust WordPress management capabilities, using Python’s subprocess module to execute WP-CLI commands from a Typer application. The integration works by defining Typer commands that correspond to WordPress tasks. These commands trigger WP-CLI operations via subprocess, capturing and processing the output for user-friendly display or further manipulation. For instance, a Typer command to list WordPress plugins might accept the WordPress installation path as an argument, run wp plugin list --format=json through subprocess, parse the JSON response, and output plugin names and statuses.
Key Considerations for Integration
To ensure a smooth and secure setup, several factors must be addressed:

[ul][li]WP-CLI Installation: WP-CLI must be installed and available in the system’s PATH.[li]WordPress Path: Specify the WordPress directory using the --path flag or run the Typer app from within it.[li]Output Handling: WP-CLI output can be captured as plain text or JSON for structured data processing.[li]Error Handling: Implement checks for command failures or parsing errors to enhance reliability.[li]Security: Pass arguments to subprocess as a list to prevent injection vulnerabilities.
Practical Use Cases
This approach supports a variety of WordPress management tasks, such as:

[ul][li]Database Backups: Automate wp db export for regular backups.[li]Plugin Updates: Run wp plugin update --all to keep plugins current.[li]User Management: Execute wp user create to add new users efficiently. These can be bundled into a single Typer app, creating a unified CLI experience.
Advanced Features
The integration can be extended with:

[ul][li]Multi-Site Management: Use configuration files or flags to manage multiple WordPress installations.[li]Remote Execution: Integrate SSH libraries like paramiko to run WP-CLI commands on remote servers.[li]Data Analysis: Parse JSON output to analyze plugin statuses or other site metrics.
Limitations
A notable constraint is that custom WP-CLI commands cannot be written in Python; the integration relies on executing existing WP-CLI commands via subprocess.
Conclusion
By combining Typer and WP-CLI, developers can craft a tailored, Python-based CLI for WordPress management, automating tasks like backups and updates. Starting with basic commands and scaling to advanced features, this method leverages both tools’ strengths, with WP-CLI’s documentation offering further command inspiration.

It is a balancing act on how far you are willing to go to perfect your tools and primitives, but ultimately it will free you up to pursue high order opportunities with confidence.

Once you have the LEGO components dial-ed in, you can move with speed to build interesting ideas... but be judicious and not try to do it all in one go.

I used Memory Bank for a few months before switching to Task Master.

Both Cline and Task Master rely on Cursor Rules to manage tasks behind the scenes.

Pick one system and master it.

Memory Bank is basically Cline’s version of Task Master.

Cline pioneered agentic workflows by shifting to a task-based system.
You work from `[projectBrief.md](http://projectBrief.md)` in Cline.
You work from `prd.txt` in Task Master.

Task Master improved on this by turning tasks into a table, allowing agents to work directly from the list.

This removed the need for a separate todo file that many Cline/Memory Bank users relied on.

The only time I find Memory Bank useful now is when starting a project you’re unfamiliar with.

It creates helpful files like `ProductContext`, `TechContext`, and `ActiveContext`, and Cline updates them as you work.

If I were you, I’d commit to either Task Master or Cline and get really good at it.

Swapping tools constantly kills momentum.

For me, Task Master is the one—I’ve used them all.

Here is an example of a gem that I use to refactor tailwindcss components into laravel blade component. Saved me a fair bit of time in a recent job. Refactor a provided Tailwind CSS HTML component into a Laravel anonymous Blade component, with additional requirements for HTML validation and text data extraction. Follow these guidelines: 1. **Component Conversion**: - Convert the provided HTML component into an anonymous Blade component, stored in the `resources/views/components` directory \(e.g., `resources/views/components/{component-name}.blade.php`\). - Preserve all Tailwind CSS classes, styling, and functionality from the original HTML. - Ensure the component is modular, reusable, and follows Laravel’s Blade component conventions \(e.g., using `x-{component-name}` syntax\). 2. **HTML Validation**: - Validate the provided HTML to ensure it is well-formed and adheres to HTML5 standards. - If the HTML contains errors \(e.g., unclosed tags, invalid attributes, or deprecated elements\), suggest corrections and apply them in the refactored Blade component. - If validation tools or libraries \(e.g., HTML5 Validator, DOMParser\) are recommended, note their use and how they ensure compliance. 3. **Text Data Extraction**: - Identify and extract all text content from the HTML component \(e.g., labels, headings, paragraphs, or button text\). - Convert extracted text into Blade component props, allowing dynamic injection of text content when the component is used. - Use meaningful prop names that reflect the purpose of the text \(e.g., `title`, `description`, `buttonText`\). - If text is repeated or context-dependent, provide fallback values or optional props using Blade’s `@props` directive with defaults \(e.g., `@props\(\['title' => 'Default Title'\]\)`\). 4. **Dynamic Data and Interactivity**: - Support dynamic data by implementing Blade slots \(e.g., `{{ $slot }}`\) or custom attributes \(e.g., `{{ $attributes }}`\) for flexible content injection. - If the component includes JavaScript for interactivity \(e.g., toggles, modals\), suggest integrating with lightweight solutions like Alpine.js or referencing external scripts, ensuring compatibility with Laravel. - Use Blade directives \(e.g., `@if`, `@foreach`, `@class`\) to handle conditional rendering, loops, or dynamic Tailwind classes as needed. 5. **Reusability and Best Practices**: - Optimize the component for reusability across different views or projects, minimizing hardcoded values and ensuring flexibility. - Follow modern Laravel \(e.g., Laravel 11\) and Tailwind CSS \(e.g., 3.x\) conventions, including support for Tailwind’s JIT compiler or custom configurations if applicable. - If the component depends on specific Tailwind plugins or themes, note how to ensure compatibility \(e.g., updating `tailwind.config.js`\). 6. **Documentation and Usage**: - Provide a brief example of how to use the refactored Blade component in a Laravel view, including: - Syntax for invoking the component \(e.g., ``\). - Passing extracted text props and any slots or attributes. - Handling dynamic or optional content. - Include a sample of the component’s props and their expected types \(e.g., string, array\) for clarity. 7. **Handling Edge Cases**: - If the provided HTML is incomplete, ambiguous, or contains non-standard elements, make reasonable assumptions about its intended functionality and document those assumptions. - If no text content is present, suggest potential props based on the component’s structure \(e.g., placeholder text for a button or card\). - If the component is complex \(e.g., nested elements, multiple text nodes\), organize props logically and consider nested slots or sub-components. 8. **Context and Clarifications**: - If additional context is needed \(e.g., Laravel version, Tailwind CSS setup, or specific validation requirements\), ask for clarification or assume best practices based on current standards. - If the component is part of a larger system \(e.g., a dashboard or form\), suggest how it integrates with other components or Laravel features \(e.g., Livewire, Inertia.js\). **Deliverables**: - The refactored anonymous Blade component code \(e.g., `resources/views/components/{component-name}.blade.php`\). - A list of extracted text props with their default values and purposes. - Validation results or corrections applied to the HTML. - An example of using the component in a Laravel view. - Any assumptions or recommendations for further optimization. **Example Input \(for clarity\)**: If the input HTML is: ```html

Welcome to Our Site

This is a sample description.

``` - Validate the HTML for correctness. - Extract text \(`Welcome to Our Site`, `This is a sample description`, `Click Me`\) into props \(e.g., `title`, `description`, `buttonText`\). - Refactor into a Blade component \(e.g., `card.blade.php`\) with props and optional slots. - Provide usage example: ``. --- ### Example Application If you provide a specific Tailwind CSS HTML component, I can: 1. Validate its HTML structure. 2. Extract text content into props \(e.g., `title`, `subtitle`, `buttonText`\). 3. Refactor it into an anonymous Blade component with proper props and slots. 4. Show how to use it in a Laravel view.

[@Parker Rex](obj://user/9e1dcceddb0a4f9db7625e2f00680a4b) Try this gem

**Role:** You are an expert Python developer with extensive knowledge of the Pillow \(PIL\) library, specializing in reverse-engineering image designs and generating high-fidelity code to replicate them. Your expertise includes precise analysis of visual elements, typography, color palettes, and image layering to produce adaptable and reusable code.

**Objective:** You are provided with a thumbnail image. Your goal is to generate high-quality, well-commented, and adaptable Python code using the Pillow library that accurately recreates the thumbnail's visual appearance. The generated code should precisely replicate the layout, fonts, colors, layer ordering, and all visual effects present in the original thumbnail. The code should be designed for maximum flexibility, allowing easy adjustments by the user.

**Input:** A thumbnail image \(provided separately\).

**Output:** A complete Python script utilizing the Pillow library.

**Detailed Instructions:**

1. **Comprehensive Image Analysis:**
* **Layer Breakdown:** Methodically identify and separate all distinct visual layers within the thumbnail. These may include background elements, foreground images, text overlays, graphical shapes, logos, and special effects. Precisely determine the stacking order \(z-order\) of these layers, as this is crucial for accurate reconstruction.
* **Background Details:** Analyze the background with great care. Determine if it is a solid color, a gradient \(including type and direction\), a tiled pattern, or a complex image. Extract color codes \(RGB, HEX\), gradient stops, pattern details, or image filenames as appropriate.
* **Text Element Extraction:** Extract all text strings. For each text element, meticulously determine the following:
* Exact font family. If an exact match is impossible, suggest several visually similar and widely available fonts, ordered by similarity.
* Font size in points.
* Font weight \(e.g., normal, bold, light\) and style \(e.g., italic, underline\).
* Precise color \(RGB, HEX\).
* Horizontal and vertical alignment.
* Position \(x, y coordinates\). Specify whether coordinates are relative to the top-left corner, center, or other reference points.
* Any text effects, including:
* Drop shadows \(color, offset, blur radius\).
* Outlines/strokes \(color, thickness\).
* Glows \(color, radius\).
* Gradients \(colors, direction\).
* Transparency/opacity.
* **Image and Graphic Element Details:** For each embedded image or distinct graphic element \(e.g., logos, icons, illustrations\):
* Note its filename \(the code should use a placeholder variable for the file path\).
* Determine its exact position, size, and aspect ratio.
* Identify any transformations \(rotation, skew\).
* Check for transparency or masking.
* Look for any applied effects \(color overlays, shadows, borders\).
* **Shape Identification:** Detect all geometric shapes \(rectangles, circles, polygons, lines, etc.\). For each shape, note:
* Type of shape.
* Dimensions.
* Position.
* Fill color \(or gradient\).
* Stroke/outline color and thickness.
* Any effects \(shadows, glows, transparency\).
* **Color Palette Analysis:** Identify all colors used in the thumbnail and extract their precise RGB or HEX values. Group them by element type \(e.g., background colors, text colors, shape fills\) for clarity in the generated code.
* **Visual Effects:** Carefully analyze the thumbnail for any overall visual effects, such as:
* Borders \(color, thickness, style\).
* Overlays \(color, blending mode, opacity\).
* Grain or noise.
* Blur or sharpening.
* Vignettes.
* Transparency/opacity applied to entire layers or elements.

2. **Precise Python Code Generation \(Pillow\):**
* **Code Structure:**
* Begin with clear comments explaining the purpose of the script and its input/output.
* Define all configuration variables at the beginning of the script for easy modification. This includes:

Absolutely, it has opened the door for many and expanded the realm of what is possible.

However, just because something is possible, does not mean that it needs to be done. For instance, I found myself vibe coding a news aggregation app to read news from various sources. One one hand, it is good as it allowed me to test drive task master and cursor and push through challenges. However, after spending an inordinate amount of time writing parsers for atom, rss ... retry mechanisms, security etc ... I realised I was over engineering and taking my eyes of the most important part goal which is serving my customers.

This post was a reminder to me and fellow vibe coders that there is still plenty of software and tools that can do the job instead of rolling out our own. It pays to spend even a few minutes to do a thorough search to see if there is something that does what you intend to build. Building an integration e.g via web hooks or API....can be a great middle ground.

As [@Deividas Paulauskas](obj://user/e0ed4d8f8956414381d577a4a765a314) rightly mentioned, maintaining software and managing technical debt must be factored in.

metadata.content:
Perfect! Yes the PRD skill, and understanding the basics of the tech you want to build products or services around is what I’d go after!

Use ai by asking tons of questions. If you want to build a web app, typescript and react is a great place to start! You can upload the typescript handbook to a GPT and have Chat GPT tasks send you lessons each morning on a timer. You can also use the fisherman prompt in the first skool module to break the topics out into step by step lessons.

That’s a nice method to PAIR with finding open source projects on github that inspire you. You clone them down to your computer and use your cursor chat to ask tons and tons of questions. How does this work? How does this connect to that? What’s that word mean? Explain like I’m 5. Explain like I’m a network engineer with XYZ skillset and make analogies to my industry.

In short + gpts trained on desired stack + OSS is a great jumping off point. Then finding a problem YOU want to solve. Then chasing that thread. It will get you through the ups and the downs. The downs are where you LEARN!

Pls reach out anytime on here or on Discord with questions. So excited to have you!

metadata.content:
Good to hear it! The product strategy happens before you write code.

I follow a simplified format from the book [shape up](https://basecamp.com/shapeup) and have for close to a decade.
[ul][li]Narrow the problem [li]Sketch out a few rough solutions to solve said problem [li]List things out of bounds \(no goes\)[li]List potential rabbit holes \(things you know could be a time bomb\) [li]Then time box it as a constraint \(less relevant - never tell the ai a time box\)

It works great for 0 -> 1 and for 1.0 to 1.1 and beyond.

I havent made videos about this ... but writing it out I realize I should

You get more leverage on your time writing code / designing if youve thought it out ahead of time.

And then you bring it into asking the AI how to further shape your idea, poke holes in it, find open questions, find where it fits into an existing codebase or where you should start if its brand new.

What HAS changed drastically is once youre in the editor...

because AI confidently paints a picture of how easy this implementation will be ...then its 4am and you're about to throw your laptop off a bridge.

So it requires having discipline around a set of steps you follow for all work.

If I spent an hour working on a new feature, I'd spend at least half that time refining the PRD. Taking that initial pitch format, doing research on tech / designs / other peoples repos I can learn from.

Then when I get to implementation, using a tool called Task Master, the majority of the intitial thinking is done. Which means the AI doesn't have to waste any valuable compute on it. Instead it plusses up and expands the idea, steel mans both sides.. and improves it.

From there you shape the idea further, actually guiding the AI to do the tasks. Making changes along the way...

And finally once you're happy with it you are now testing it locally.

A massive benefit of AI is making the 'testing' part of coding fun.

I rolled out a set of automations for my youtube videos that have 4 separate sets of tests. 4! I would've never done that without AI. Now its ready for any scale of traffic

Message me on Discord or on here and let's get your project off the ground. Need to know where you are at with it, and some other details.

Again happy to have you! Sorry for the long winded answer.

metadata.content:
Good to hear it! The product strategy happens before you write code.

I follow a simplified format from the book [shape up](https://basecamp.com/shapeup) and have for close to a decade.
[ul][li]Narrow the problem [li]Sketch out a few rough solutions to solve said problem [li]List things out of bounds \(no goes\)[li]List potential rabbit holes \(things you know could be a time bomb\) [li]Then time box it as a constraint \(less relevant - never tell the ai a time box\)

It works great for 0 -> 1 and for 1.0 to 1.1 and beyond.

I havent made videos about this ... but writing it out I realize I should

You get more leverage on your time writing code / designing if youve thought it out ahead of time.

And then you bring it into asking the AI how to further shape your idea, poke holes in it, find open questions, find where it fits into an existing codebase or where you should start if its brand new.

What HAS changed drastically is once youre in the editor...

because AI confidently paints a picture of how easy this implementation will be ...then its 4am and you're about to throw your laptop off a bridge.

So it requires having discipline around a set of steps you follow for all work.

If I spent an hour working on a new feature, I'd spend at least half that time refining the PRD. Taking that initial pitch format, doing research on tech / designs / other peoples repos I can learn from.

Then when I get to implementation, using a tool called Task Master, the majority of the intitial thinking is done. Which means the AI doesn't have to waste any valuable compute on it. Instead it plusses up and expands the idea, steel mans both sides.. and improves it.

From there you shape the idea further, actually guiding the AI to do the tasks. Making changes along the way...

And finally once you're happy with it you are now testing it locally.

A massive benefit of AI is making the 'testing' part of coding fun.

I rolled out a set of automations for my youtube videos that have 4 separate sets of tests. 4! I would've never done that without AI. Now its ready for any scale of traffic

Message me on Discord or on here and let's get your project off the ground. Need to know where you are at with it, and some other details.

Again happy to have you! Sorry for the long winded answer.

metadata.bio: Exploring making youtubes

metadata.content:
Good to hear it! The product strategy happens before you write code.

I follow a simplified format from the book [shape up](https://basecamp.com/shapeup) and have for close to a decade.
[ul][li]Narrow the problem [li]Sketch out a few rough solutions to solve said problem [li]List things out of bounds \(no goes\)[li]List potential rabbit holes \(things you know could be a time bomb\) [li]Then time box it as a constraint \(less relevant - never tell the ai a time box\)

It works great for 0 -> 1 and for 1.0 to 1.1 and beyond.

I havent made videos about this ... but writing it out I realize I should

You get more leverage on your time writing code / designing if youve thought it out ahead of time.

And then you bring it into asking the AI how to further shape your idea, poke holes in it, find open questions, find where it fits into an existing codebase or where you should start if its brand new.

What HAS changed drastically is once youre in the editor...

because AI confidently paints a picture of how easy this implementation will be ...then its 4am and you're about to throw your laptop off a bridge.

So it requires having discipline around a set of steps you follow for all work.

If I spent an hour working on a new feature, I'd spend at least half that time refining the PRD. Taking that initial pitch format, doing research on tech / designs / other peoples repos I can learn from.

Then when I get to implementation, using a tool called Task Master, the majority of the intitial thinking is done. Which means the AI doesn't have to waste any valuable compute on it. Instead it plusses up and expands the idea, steel mans both sides.. and improves it.

From there you shape the idea further, actually guiding the AI to do the tasks. Making changes along the way...

And finally once you're happy with it you are now testing it locally.

A massive benefit of AI is making the 'testing' part of coding fun.

I rolled out a set of automations for my youtube videos that have 4 separate sets of tests. 4! I would've never done that without AI. Now its ready for any scale of traffic

Message me on Discord or on here and let's get your project off the ground. Need to know where you are at with it, and some other details.

Again happy to have you! Sorry for the long winded answer.

metadata.content:
Good to hear it! The product strategy happens before you write code.

I follow a simplified format from the book [shape up](https://basecamp.com/shapeup) and have for close to a decade.
[ul][li]Narrow the problem [li]Sketch out a few rough solutions to solve said problem [li]List things out of bounds \(no goes\)[li]List potential rabbit holes \(things you know could be a time bomb\) [li]Then time box it as a constraint \(less relevant - never tell the ai a time box\)

It works great for 0 -> 1 and for 1.0 to 1.1 and beyond.

I havent made videos about this ... but writing it out I realize I should

You get more leverage on your time writing code / designing if youve thought it out ahead of time.

And then you bring it into asking the AI how to further shape your idea, poke holes in it, find open questions, find where it fits into an existing codebase or where you should start if its brand new.

What HAS changed drastically is once youre in the editor...

because AI confidently paints a picture of how easy this implementation will be ...then its 4am and you're about to throw your laptop off a bridge.

So it requires having discipline around a set of steps you follow for all work.

If I spent an hour working on a new feature, I'd spend at least half that time refining the PRD. Taking that initial pitch format, doing research on tech / designs / other peoples repos I can learn from.

Then when I get to implementation, using a tool called Task Master, the majority of the intitial thinking is done. Which means the AI doesn't have to waste any valuable compute on it. Instead it plusses up and expands the idea, steel mans both sides.. and improves it.

From there you shape the idea further, actually guiding the AI to do the tasks. Making changes along the way...

And finally once you're happy with it you are now testing it locally.

A massive benefit of AI is making the 'testing' part of coding fun.

I rolled out a set of automations for my youtube videos that have 4 separate sets of tests. 4! I would've never done that without AI. Now its ready for any scale of traffic

Message me on Discord or on here and let's get your project off the ground. Need to know where you are at with it, and some other details.

Again happy to have you! Sorry for the long winded answer.

metadata.content:
Good to hear it! The product strategy happens before you write code.

I follow a simplified format from the book [shape up](https://basecamp.com/shapeup) and have for close to a decade.
[ul][li]Narrow the problem [li]Sketch out a few rough solutions to solve said problem [li]List things out of bounds \(no goes\)[li]List potential rabbit holes \(things you know could be a time bomb\) [li]Then time box it as a constraint \(less relevant - never tell the ai a time box\)

It works great for 0 -> 1 and for 1.0 to 1.1 and beyond.

I havent made videos about this ... but writing it out I realize I should

You get more leverage on your time writing code / designing if youve thought it out ahead of time.

And then you bring it into asking the AI how to further shape your idea, poke holes in it, find open questions, find where it fits into an existing codebase or where you should start if its brand new.

What HAS changed drastically is once youre in the editor...

because AI confidently paints a picture of how easy this implementation will be ...then its 4am and you're about to throw your laptop off a bridge.

So it requires having discipline around a set of steps you follow for all work.

If I spent an hour working on a new feature, I'd spend at least half that time refining the PRD. Taking that initial pitch format, doing research on tech / designs / other peoples repos I can learn from.

Then when I get to implementation, using a tool called Task Master, the majority of the intitial thinking is done. Which means the AI doesn't have to waste any valuable compute on it. Instead it plusses up and expands the idea, steel mans both sides.. and improves it.

From there you shape the idea further, actually guiding the AI to do the tasks. Making changes along the way...

And finally once you're happy with it you are now testing it locally.

A massive benefit of AI is making the 'testing' part of coding fun.

I rolled out a set of automations for my youtube videos that have 4 separate sets of tests. 4! I would've never done that without AI. Now its ready for any scale of traffic

Message me on Discord or on here and let's get your project off the ground. Need to know where you are at with it, and some other details.

Again happy to have you! Sorry for the long winded answer.

Using Typer and WP-CLI Together: A Concise Guide
Typer, a Python library for building command-line interfaces \(CLIs\), and WP-CLI, a PHP-based tool for managing WordPress sites, can be integrated to create a powerful, custom CLI for WordPress administration. This combination harnesses Python’s flexibility and WP-CLI’s robust WordPress management capabilities, using Python’s subprocess module to execute WP-CLI commands from a Typer application. The integration works by defining Typer commands that correspond to WordPress tasks. These commands trigger WP-CLI operations via subprocess, capturing and processing the output for user-friendly display or further manipulation. For instance, a Typer command to list WordPress plugins might accept the WordPress installation path as an argument, run wp plugin list --format=json through subprocess, parse the JSON response, and output plugin names and statuses.
Key Considerations for Integration
To ensure a smooth and secure setup, several factors must be addressed:

[ul][li]WP-CLI Installation: WP-CLI must be installed and available in the system’s PATH.[li]WordPress Path: Specify the WordPress directory using the --path flag or run the Typer app from within it.[li]Output Handling: WP-CLI output can be captured as plain text or JSON for structured data processing.[li]Error Handling: Implement checks for command failures or parsing errors to enhance reliability.[li]Security: Pass arguments to subprocess as a list to prevent injection vulnerabilities.
Practical Use Cases
This approach supports a variety of WordPress management tasks, such as:

[ul][li]Database Backups: Automate wp db export for regular backups.[li]Plugin Updates: Run wp plugin update --all to keep plugins current.[li]User Management: Execute wp user create to add new users efficiently. These can be bundled into a single Typer app, creating a unified CLI experience.
Advanced Features
The integration can be extended with:

[ul][li]Multi-Site Management: Use configuration files or flags to manage multiple WordPress installations.[li]Remote Execution: Integrate SSH libraries like paramiko to run WP-CLI commands on remote servers.[li]Data Analysis: Parse JSON output to analyze plugin statuses or other site metrics.
Limitations
A notable constraint is that custom WP-CLI commands cannot be written in Python; the integration relies on executing existing WP-CLI commands via subprocess.
Conclusion
By combining Typer and WP-CLI, developers can craft a tailored, Python-based CLI for WordPress management, automating tasks like backups and updates. Starting with basic commands and scaling to advanced features, this method leverages both tools’ strengths, with WP-CLI’s documentation offering further command inspiration.

metadata.content: Appreciate you making a recording for those of us who can't make the timeslot

I used Memory Bank for a few months before switching to Task Master.

Both Cline and Task Master rely on Cursor Rules to manage tasks behind the scenes.

Pick one system and master it.

Memory Bank is basically Cline’s version of Task Master.

Cline pioneered agentic workflows by shifting to a task-based system.
You work from `[projectBrief.md](http://projectBrief.md)` in Cline.
You work from `prd.txt` in Task Master.

Task Master improved on this by turning tasks into a table, allowing agents to work directly from the list.

This removed the need for a separate todo file that many Cline/Memory Bank users relied on.

The only time I find Memory Bank useful now is when starting a project you’re unfamiliar with.

It creates helpful files like `ProductContext`, `TechContext`, and `ActiveContext`, and Cline updates them as you work.

If I were you, I’d commit to either Task Master or Cline and get really good at it.

Swapping tools constantly kills momentum.

For me, Task Master is the one—I’ve used them all.

Here is an example of a gem that I use to refactor tailwindcss components into laravel blade component. Saved me a fair bit of time in a recent job. Refactor a provided Tailwind CSS HTML component into a Laravel anonymous Blade component, with additional requirements for HTML validation and text data extraction. Follow these guidelines: 1. **Component Conversion**: - Convert the provided HTML component into an anonymous Blade component, stored in the `resources/views/components` directory \(e.g., `resources/views/components/{component-name}.blade.php`\). - metadata.content:
Perfect! Yes the PRD skill, and understanding the basics of the tech you want to build products or services around is what I’d go after!

Use ai by asking tons of questions. If you want to build a web app, typescript and react is a great place to start! You can upload the typescript handbook to a GPT and have Chat GPT tasks send you lessons each morning on a timer. You can also use the fisherman prompt in the first skool module to break the topics out into step by step lessons.

That’s a nice method to PAIR with finding open source projects on github that inspire you. You clone them down to your computer and use your cursor chat to ask tons and tons of questions. How does this work? How does this connect to that? What’s that word mean? Explain like I’m 5. Explain like I’m a network engineer with XYZ skillset and make analogies to my industry.

In short + gpts trained on desired stack + OSS is a great jumping off point. Then finding a problem YOU want to solve. Then chasing that thread. It will get you through the ups and the downs. The downs are where you LEARN!

Pls reach out anytime on here or on Discord with questions. So excited to have you!

metadata.content:
Actually I have another client that's a product distributor. It's an absolute pain making new product codes for them because different products have different specs. The product codes are stored in a table \(below\). Every time a new product is introduced we have to think up a way to fit the important data about the product into the existing table structure. It would be wildly helpful if...
1.\) An agent could gather the necessary information and then create the product code automatically.
2.\) The data could be managed in such a way that agents could store relevant data dynamically. I.e. cups have 5 spec fields, spoons have 3, so the database doesn't have a bunch of blank fields.

Hope that makes sense!
+-----------------------+
| Column Name |
+-----------------------+
| id |
| product_code |
| description |
| created_at |

metadata.content:
They serve different roles. n8n is no code automation like [make.com](http://make.com)

Mermaid is for graphing, and you rely on LLMs to create the graphs so that you can better visualize a system like a codebase or a database schema.

For most coding/system architecture tasks you still want to know the basics so that you can get a higher multiple on your skills.
